newsitem.title: MADAGASCAR: France sends aid by air to cyclone-hit Madagascar.
newsitem.headline: France sends aid by air to cyclone-hit Madagascar.

text.p: The French military was sending a plane, a helicopter and rescue workers to Madagascar on Monday to search for more than 100 dead and missing from a cyclone and help more than 30,000 homeless, officials said.
They said the helicopter and a Transall transport plane carrying rescue workers firemen, doctors and other experts were expected to arrive from the French garrison on the island of Reunion.
They said the helicopter was a key for relief efforts because many roads on the southern tip of Madagascar were cut.
State radio said radio messages from the south indicated many more than 100 people were killed or missing and more than 30,000 people were homeless.
It said in Farafangana district, hit with the full force of Cyclone Gretelle packing winds of up to 250 km (155 miles per hour) on Friday night, no one has shelter.
"In Farafangana town, all 27,500 residents are without shelter," said a correspondent for the radio in the area.
Cyclone Gretelle was the worst to hit Madagascar in living memory.
The first planeload of aid reached the south on Sunday from Antananarivo and landed in the southeastern port of Manakara, the only place in the region left with telephone links to the capital.
The radio said convoys of trucks ferrying food, medicine and building materials were finding it difficult to reach hardest-hit areas because roads were blocked in many places.
It estimated that settlements in the southeast which were hit the lightest were still at least 70 percent destroyed while many villages were almost wiped off the map by the disaster.
It said residents on the banks were watching swollen rivers for bodies swept away by floods.
Transport Minister Andre Rasolo said government buildings in the southeast were not functioning and belatedly urged residents to follow carefully radio warnings about approaching cyclones.
He asked residents to stay calm because authorities were working to help them. The radio said a team from the French electricity company was also on its way to help Madagascar.
Madagascar's foreign minister said on Sunday he had invited foreign and U.N. representatives to visit the area to assess what was most urgently needed to help the homeless.
Many villagers survived by clinging to trees to avoid being blown away. Others escaped being swept away by raging floodwaters by taking to the roofs of some buildings.
The cyclone wreaked havoc in a rich farming zone producing coffee, bananas, oranges and lychees. On Monday, it was centred southwest of Madagascar and moving towards South Africa.
Radio Madagascar has criticised the slow pace of a rescue effort and some residents said the radio failed to forecast accurately the force with which the cyclone would batter the island.
Gretelle was the seventh tropical storm to hit the former French colony since the start of the cyclone season in October.
